vids.desc: Students will become young detectives and learn how to stay safe from banking frauds. Through real-life examples, they will understand how fake calls, messages, and links trick people into sharing personal information. Students will learn the golden rule — never share PINs, OTPs, or bank details — and use decision-making skills to check whether a message is real or fake. By the end, they will know how to protect themselves and their families from fraud.

quiz.nm: Can a call steal your money? 📞

qs.q: What is a fraud call?

opts.1: A call from a friend asking for help.
opts.2: A call pretending to be from a bank asking for your PIN.
opts.3: A call from your teacher reminding about homework.

qs.q: Why should you not click on a link in a message asking for bank details?

opts.1: It might take you to a fun game.
opts.2: It might connect you to your friend.
opts.3: It might be a trick to steal your information.

qs.q: What should you do if someone asks for your ATM PIN over the phone?

opts.1: Do not share it and tell an adult.
opts.2: Write it down and keep it in your bag.
opts.3: Share it quickly to keep your account safe.

qs.q: Your friend gets a message saying they won a prize and need to click a link to claim it. What should they do to stay safe?

opts.1: Click the link right away to claim the prize.
opts.2: Ask a trusted adult if the message is real before clicking.
opts.3: Share the message with as many friends as possible.

qs.q: You receive a call from someone saying they are from your bank and need your account number to fix an issue. What is the best decision?

opts.1: Hang up and tell a trusted adult about the call.
opts.2: Give them the information quickly.
opts.3: Ignore the call and continue playing.

opts.3: Simple interest because it is easier to calculate.

qs.q: Rohan wants to buy a new bike, and he plans to save money in a bank to earn interest. His friend suggests spending the money now instead. What is the best decision for Rohan?

opts.1: Spend the money on something else.
opts.2: Save the money in the bank to earn interest for the bike.
opts.3: Lend the money to a friend.

assigns.desc: In this activity, students learn the concept of interest—the extra money a bank gives when they save. Through a child-friendly example comparing a piggy bank to a real bank, students understand how Simple Interest works as a fixed amount earned every year. Students then complete a fill-in-the-blank exercise and draw a picture of something they want to save for, helping them connect interest to real-life goals in a fun and creative way.

steps.label: Emoji response
steps.guided_text: Send a ⭐ if you feel confident, or 👎 if you are confused
steps.unguided_text: Please send any emoji of your choice!
steps.invalid_criteria: Any emoji other than ⭐ or 👎

steps.label: Word/voice reflection
steps.guided_text: What do you get from the bank when you save money, then either type your answer in a single word or send a voice note.
steps.unguided_text: What do you think of the activity? Share in one word or send a voice note
steps.valid_criteria: If the student types the word: Interest, then the response is valid OR If the student sends a voice note and the response includes the word: Interest, then the response is valid → Any 1 of the above criteria must be fulfilled
steps.invalid_criteria: If the response contains unrelated words OR If the voice note does not include the word: Interest, then the response is invalid

steps.label: Observation/image
steps.guided_text: Click a photo of something you like and upload it
steps.unguided_text: Click any picture around you and share it!
steps.invalid_criteria:
Blur image / blank / no photo

Anything other than a Clear object photo

steps.label: Voice/text
steps.unguided_text: Type or send a voice note & explain what interest means

steps.label: image/video
steps.unguided_text: Click a clear photo of your Interest activity work and upload it
